newsitem.title: USA: Tainted berries lead to San Diego fraud charges.
newsitem.headline: Tainted berries lead to San Diego fraud charges.

text.p: A food company executive was to be arraigned Wednesday on charges he defrauded the federal school lunch program when he sold it contaminated frozen strawberries from Mexico.
The program stipulates that only domestic crops may be used for the free lunches. The strawberries were linked to an outbreak of hepatitis A in Michigan.

Andrew & Williamson Sales Co. and Fred Williamson, its president, were named in a 47-count federal grand jury indictment based on the sale of Mexican strawberries to a U.S. Department of Agriculture program, the U.S. attorney general's office said.

Williamson, who could face up to five years' imprisonment, will plead not guilty, his attorney, Howard Frank, told the Los Angeles Times. The company and Williamson are charged with one count of defrauding the United States, three counts of false statements and 43 counts of false claims.

Company executives denied the charges in a statement but a company salesman, Richard Kershaw, pleaded guilty May 21 to making false statements in the sale of misbranded strawberries to the Agriculture Department. His plea was disclosed Tuesday.
Kershaw, former head of the frozen strawberry sales division, supplied information leading to the indictment and will be sentenced in August, U.S. Attorney Alan Bersin said.

"What the indictment shows is that the government investigation tracked information from a variety of sources, including the food broker involved, customs records from Mexico to the United States and shipping records, as well as documents form the company," Phillip Halpern, the lead prosecutor in the case, said.

Halpern said Kershaw's guilty plea "outlines the full scope of the scheme and implicates his co-conspirators." He added, "In that regard, he's certainly a witness able to testify to what happened from the inside."

The indictment followed a two-month investigation of the strawberry contamination, which caused 198 students and teachers in Michigan to fall ill in March. It also led to the testing for hepatitis A of as many as 9,000 students and teachers in Los Angeles.
